title: Handling Basic Objections
subtitle: How to acknowledge, understand, and respond to a prospect's concerns without losing the conversation
description: Learn how to handle common sales objections with empathy and confidence — how to acknowledge a concern, find out what is really behind it, and respond in a way that keeps the conversation moving without dismissing what the prospect feels.
dialogueSubtitle: Marcus raises several concerns before committing — Riley handles each one without becoming defensive

vocabulary.definition: A reason a prospect gives for not moving forward — a concern, doubt, or barrier that needs to be addressed before they can commit.
vocabulary.example: An objection is not a rejection — it is a signal that the prospect is still engaged but needs something resolved before they feel ready to move.

vocabulary.definition: A worry or doubt that is preventing someone from making a decision — something that feels unresolved or risky to them.
vocabulary.example: The most common concerns in B2B sales are price, timing, and risk — but the real concern is often something different beneath the surface.

vocabulary.definition: To acknowledge that a concern or objection is legitimate and understandable — not to agree with it, but to show you take it seriously.
vocabulary.example: Validating an objection does not mean you are conceding the point — it means the prospect feels heard, which makes them far more open to your response.

vocabulary.definition: To present an objection or situation from a different angle — showing it in a new light that reduces its impact or makes it easier to work with.
vocabulary.example: When a prospect says 'it is too expensive', reframe the conversation around the cost of not solving the problem — not just the cost of the solution.

vocabulary.definition: To show genuine understanding of how the prospect feels — not just what they are saying, but why it matters to them.
vocabulary.example: Empathising with a concern is not the same as agreeing with it — it signals that you understand their world well enough to take their hesitation seriously.

vocabulary.definition: A delaying tactic — when a prospect gives a vague reason for not deciding, without saying no directly. Usually a sign that something else is unresolved.
vocabulary.example: 'We will think about it' is often a stall rather than a genuine objection — the real issue is usually that the value is not yet clear or the risk feels too high.

vocabulary.definition: To successfully address an objection so that it is no longer a barrier — not by arguing, but by providing what the prospect needs to feel confident.
vocabulary.example: You do not overcome an objection by talking louder or pushing harder — you overcome it by understanding what is really behind it and addressing that specific thing.

vocabulary.definition: To deal with a concern directly and specifically — to give it the attention it deserves rather than deflecting or moving past it.
vocabulary.example: When a prospect raises a concern, address it before moving on — skipping over it signals that you did not listen, or that you have no good answer.

phrasalVerbs.definition: The core acknowledgment phrase — opens your response by showing the prospect that their worry has been heard and taken seriously, before you say anything else.
phrasalVerbs.example: I understand your concern about the timeline — that is a completely reasonable thing to raise at this stage. Can I share how other teams in a similar position have handled the rollout?

phrasalVerbs.phrase: CAN I ASK WHAT IS BEHIND THAT
phrasalVerbs.definition: Probe the objection before responding — find out what is really driving the concern so you can address the actual issue, not just the surface statement.
phrasalVerbs.example: When you say the timing is not right — can I ask what is behind that? I want to make sure I understand whether it is a capacity issue, a budget cycle, or something else.

phrasalVerbs.definition: Validate the objection without fully conceding — acknowledges the legitimacy of what the prospect has said while keeping the door open for your response.
phrasalVerbs.example: That is a fair point — the price is higher than some alternatives. What I would say is that the comparison only makes sense if the alternatives actually solve the same problem.

phrasalVerbs.phrase: WHAT I HEAR YOU SAYING IS
phrasalVerbs.definition: Reflect back the objection in your own words — confirms you have understood it correctly and gives the prospect a chance to clarify before you respond.
phrasalVerbs.example: What I hear you saying is that the value is clear but the timing feels wrong given everything else the team has on right now. Is that a fair summary?

phrasalVerbs.definition: Signal that you are going to tackle the concern head-on — builds confidence that you are not going to deflect or dodge the difficult question.
phrasalVerbs.example: Let me address that directly — yes, there is an implementation period, and yes, it requires some time from the team. Here is what that actually looks like in practice.

phrasalVerbs.definition: Turn a stall or soft no into actionable information — asks the prospect to define what would need to be true for them to move forward.
phrasalVerbs.example: I hear you — what would it take for this to feel like the right move? I want to understand what is still unresolved so I can either address it or tell you honestly if I cannot.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: So — based on everything we have covered, does this feel like the right direction for the team?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Honestly, yes — but I have a few [[concern:a worry or doubt that is preventing someone from making a decision]]s I want to raise before we go any further.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Please — I would rather hear them now than after. What is on your mind?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: First — the price. It is higher than I was expecting for the pipeline plan.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: I understand your [[concern:a worry or doubt that is preventing someone from making a decision]] — price is always a fair thing to raise. That is a fair point and I am not going to pretend it is cheap. Can I ask what is behind it — is it the absolute number, or is it more about being able to justify it internally?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Mainly the internal justification. I would need to show the board why this makes sense.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: What I hear you saying is that the value is clear to you, but you need to [[address:to deal with a concern directly and specifically]] it for the people who have not been in this conversation. Is that right?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Exactly. I need to [[validate:to acknowledge that a concern is legitimate]] their concerns too, not just my own.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Let me address that directly — we have a one-page business case template I can customise for you, built around the numbers you gave me. Two to three deals a month at your deal size — that becomes very easy to justify. What is the second concern?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Timing. Q4 is always chaotic — I am not sure this is the right moment to [[overcome:to successfully address an objection so it is no longer a barrier]] the internal resistance and launch something new.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: I [[empathise:to show genuine understanding of how the prospect feels]] with that — Q4 is genuinely difficult for this kind of change. Let me [[reframe:to present something from a different angle to reduce its impact]] it slightly: you are currently losing deals every month because of this problem. A two-week setup now recovers some of those Q4 deals. Waiting until January means another quarter of the same [[stall:a delaying tactic when a prospect gives a vague reason without deciding]]. Does that change how the timing feels?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: It does — when you put it that way. What would it take to get started quickly without it feeling like a big disruption?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: That is exactly the right question — and I think you will like the answer.

registerAwareness.example: 'I understand your concern — price is always worth raising. That is a fair point. Can I ask what is behind it — is it the number itself, or is it more about justifying it internally? Because those are two very different conversations.'

registerAwareness.context: Written response to a price objection by email
registerAwareness.example: 'Thank you for raising the pricing concern — I want to address it directly. Based on the figures we discussed (two to three deals per month at your average deal size), the ROI becomes clear within the first quarter. I have attached a brief business case that may help with internal sign-off.'

'Hey Marcus — I know you said you needed to think about it. I just wanted to check in properly rather than just send a chase email. What is actually behind the hesitation? I would rather know than guess.'

'I understand the board's concern about implementation risk — let me address that directly. Our average onboarding time for a team of this size is eleven days, and we assign a dedicated implementation manager for the first thirty days. I can share reference customers of similar scale if that would be helpful.'

Objections raised: (1) price — board justification needed, not budget. Sending business case template. (2) Q4 timing — addressed with cost-of-delay argument, responded positively. (3) implementation risk — not raised directly but likely underlying. Prepare case studies for next call.

registerTraps: ❌ Responding to an objection before you have fully understood it is one of the most common mistakes in sales — ask what is behind it first. You might be addressing the wrong concern entirely.
✅ 'I understand your concern' only works if what follows shows you actually do. Saying it and then immediately contradicting the concern signals the opposite of empathy.
🔁 A stall ('let us think about it', 'not right now') is not an objection — it usually means something is still unresolved. Ask 'what would it take?' to find out what is really going on.
💡 The goal of objection handling is not to win the argument — it is to find out what the prospect needs to feel confident. Address that specific thing, not a general version of the objection.

multipleChoiceExercise.question: What is the first thing Riley does when Marcus raises his price concern?
options: She explains why Brightline is worth the price
She offers a discount
She acknowledges the concern and asks what is behind it — is it the number or the internal justification?
She moves the conversation to the next topic

multipleChoiceExercise.question: What does Riley mean when she says 'what I hear you saying is'?
options: She is repeating Marcus's words back to him to confirm she understood the objection correctly
She is summarising the whole conversation so far
She is challenging whether Marcus's concern is valid
She is preparing to move to the next slide in her demo

multipleChoiceExercise.question: How does Riley handle Marcus's timing objection about Q4?
options: She agrees and suggests waiting until Q1
She reframes it — pointing out that the cost of waiting is losing deals every month
She offers a shorter contract to reduce the risk
She asks Marcus to speak to other customers about how they handled the timing

multipleChoiceExercise.question: What is a 'stall' in a sales context?
options: When a deal is stuck because of a pricing dispute
When a prospect gives a vague delaying reason without saying yes or no directly
When a salesperson takes too long to respond to an objection
When a contract negotiation goes on for more than a month

multipleChoiceExercise.question: What does Riley offer to help Marcus justify the price to the board?
options: A free trial period
A reference call with another customer
A customised one-page business case built around the deal loss numbers Marcus shared
A discounted enterprise rate

multipleChoiceExercise.question: According to the Register Traps, what is wrong with 'I understand your concern' followed by an immediate contradiction?
options: It is grammatically incorrect to use 'understand' with 'concern'
It signals the opposite of empathy — it shows you said the words but did not actually mean them
It is too informal for a B2B sales conversation
It gives the prospect permission to raise more objections

multipleChoiceExercise.question: What is the purpose of 'what would it take' as a phrase?
options: To find out the prospect's budget
To challenge whether their objection is reasonable
To turn a stall or vague no into specific, actionable information about what is unresolved
To ask the prospect to make a final decision

multipleChoiceExercise.question: What is the key difference between validating an objection and conceding it?
options: There is no difference — validating an objection means you agree with it
Validating acknowledges the concern as legitimate without agreeing; conceding means you accept it as a reason not to proceed
Conceding is more professional in formal enterprise settings
Validating is only appropriate for price objections

chooseResponse.instructions: Work in groups. A prospect has raised an objection. Choose the response that handles it most effectively — acknowledges the concern, probes where needed, and keeps the conversation moving. Discuss before clicking.

items.customerLine: Prospect says: 'Your price is just too high compared to what we are paying now.'
options: Say: 'I understand your concern — let me address that directly. Can I ask what is behind it? Is it the absolute cost, or is it more about being able to justify the difference internally?'
Say: 'I understand, but our product is genuinely better — the extra cost reflects the extra value you get.'
Say: 'We do offer a discount for annual contracts — would that help?'
items.explanation: A is correct. It acknowledges the concern, then probes before responding — because 'too expensive' can mean very different things. B jumps to a defence of the price without understanding what the real concern is. C offers a discount immediately, which signals that the price was inflated to begin with and sets a bad precedent for the negotiation.

items.customerLine: Prospect says: 'We are actually already using a competitor's tool.'
options: Say: 'That is a fair point. Can I ask what is behind the decision to look at alternatives — is there something the current tool is not doing for you?'
Say: 'That is fine — a lot of our customers came from that tool. Ours is better.'
Say: 'I understand — in that case, maybe now is not the right time for us to speak.'
items.explanation: A is correct. The fact that they are already talking to you means something is not quite right with the current tool — find out what. That is the real conversation. B makes a direct comparison claim before you understand the situation, which can come across as arrogant. C exits the conversation too early — the prospect is clearly open to alternatives or they would not be on the call.

items.customerLine: Prospect says: 'We had a bad experience with a similar tool two years ago and the team still talks about it.'
options: Say: 'I empathise with that — a failed rollout is genuinely painful and the trust damage lasts a long time. Can I ask what went wrong? I want to understand whether the problem was the tool, the implementation, or something else — because that changes how I would approach this with you.'
Say: 'I understand your concern — but our tool is different. We have much better onboarding support.'
Say: 'That is a fair point. Would it help to speak to some of our existing customers?'
items.explanation: A is correct. It empathises genuinely with the experience, then probes the root cause — because how you handle this depends entirely on what went wrong. If the last tool failed because of poor adoption, that is a different conversation than if it failed because of a technical mismatch. B claims differentiation before understanding the problem. C jumps to social proof — useful later, but premature before the real concern has been explored.

items.customerLine: Prospect says: 'I need to run this by my manager before we can make any decision.'
options: Say: 'Of course — what would be most helpful: should I put together a brief summary you could share, or would it make sense to include your manager in a short call?'
Say: 'I understand — who is your manager? Can I reach out to them directly?'
Say: 'Of course. What is the best timeline for that conversation? I want to make sure we keep the momentum going.'
items.explanation: A is correct. It accepts the need gracefully and immediately offers to help move it forward — two clear options, both of which keep you involved. B asks to go around the prospect to reach their manager directly, which will damage the relationship and trust. C accepts the delay and asks about timing, which is passive — it leaves the next step entirely in the prospect's hands.

profileMatch.instructions: Read the three objections. As a group, match each one to the handling approach that fits best. Think about what is really behind each objection before deciding. Click 'Check Matches' when you agree.

profiles.name: Objection 1
profiles.description: 'We would love to move forward, but honestly the timing just is not right — we are in the middle of a big project and the team does not have bandwidth for anything new until at least February.'

profiles.name: Objection 2
profiles.description: 'I like what I am hearing, but I am going to be honest — I have heard similar things from two other vendors this month and I am not sure I believe the ROI numbers are real.'

profiles.name: Objection 3
profiles.description: 'Look, we will think about it and come back to you. We are just not ready to make a decision right now.'

options.label: Reframe the cost of waiting
options.description: The prospect is using timing as a reason to delay — but delay has a cost too. Reframe the conversation: 'I understand the bandwidth concern. What I would ask is — what is the cost of waiting another quarter? If the problem is still active, the delay has a price.' Then help them see whether a low-disruption start is possible.

options.label: Validate and provide evidence
options.description: That is a fair point — healthy scepticism about ROI claims is reasonable. Address it directly: 'I would rather earn your trust than ask you to take my word for it. Let me share a case study from a team of similar size with the actual numbers, and let us look at what the calculation would look like based on your specific situation.'

options.label: Ask what would it take
options.description: 'I hear you — and I want to respect that. Before we leave it there, can I ask: what would it take for this to feel like the right move? I want to understand what is still unresolved — either so I can address it, or so I can tell you honestly if I cannot.'

finishTheLine.instructions: The salesperson has started handling an objection — but the line has been cut off. Finish it using phrases and vocabulary from this lesson. Compare your versions, then click to see a suggested answer.

items.customerLine: Prospect: 'It is just not the right time for us to take this on.'
items.salespersonStart: I understand your concern — can I ask
items.suggestedCompletion: what is behind the timing? I want to make sure I understand whether it is a capacity issue with the team right now, or something in the budget cycle. Because those are two different conversations, and I want to make sure I am addressing the right one.

items.customerLine: Prospect: 'The price is higher than what we budgeted for.'
items.salespersonStart: That is a fair point — let me address that directly.
items.suggestedCompletion: The price reflects the full pipeline visibility and automation — but I want to check: is the issue the budget itself, or is it more that you need to justify the difference to someone internally? Because if it is the latter, I can help you build that case using the numbers you gave me.

items.customerLine: Prospect: 'I am just not sure the team will adopt it — we have tried this kind of thing before.'
items.salespersonStart: I empathise with that — what I hear you saying is
items.suggestedCompletion: that the risk is not really about the tool, it is about whether people will actually use it. Is that right? Because that changes how I would approach the rollout conversation. The tools that fail usually fail at adoption, not at the product level — and that is something we handle very deliberately in the onboarding.

items.customerLine: Prospect gives a vague 'we will think about it' with no specific reason.
items.salespersonStart: I completely respect that — before we leave it there,
items.suggestedCompletion: what would it take for this to feel like the right move? I want to understand what is still unresolved — either so I can address it properly, or so I can tell you honestly if there is something I cannot help with. I would rather know now than in six weeks.
